Hi Alex —

Thanks again for the demo earlier — great conversation. Per our call, I wanted to capture the performance/SLO items and proposed next steps so we can quickly qualify fit and schedule a short load test. Summary below:

Requirements you called out (please confirm/correct):
- Latency SLOs:
  - First-token (stream start) p95 <= 250ms
  - End-to-end completion p95 <= 2s for the short-form responses we showed
- Throughput / bursts:
  - Sustained throughput: ~200 requests/min (~3.3 RPS)
  - Expected bursts: up to 600 requests/min (~10 RPS) during campaigns
- Concurrency / streaming:
  - Typical active concurrent streams: 60
  - Peak concurrent during burst: ~120 (Alex to confirm)
  - Streaming: require chunked streaming with keep-alive up to 120s and partial-update semantics preserved
- Failure/queueing behavior:
  - Want predictable queueing and graceful degradation (rate-limited shedding or fallback to smaller model variant) rather than opaque 5xx spikes

Autoscaling discussion items we want to validate with you:
- Scale-up time targets: you prefer scale-up to be transparent to customers for ~90% of spikes. If we rely on cold spin-up, warm-up times can be 45–90s depending on model/hardware.
- Warm pool / prewarmed capacity: recommended to keep a warm pool sized to 2x baseline for marketing/campaign spikes (configurable).
- Queueing policy: how long to queue requests before returning error vs. fallback behavior — we should align on max queue depth and timeout semantics.

Next steps I propose:
1) You send your recent 24–72h traffic profile (sample CSV or a short summary) — Alex said he'll share a CSV.
2) Our SE (David) will propose a recommended warm-pool + autoscale policy and the expected tail-latency numbers for your profile.
3) Schedule a 60m controlled load test in our staging region (us-west) — we can provide a prefilled test plan and a staging API key.
4) If load test looks good, we’ll add a draft mutual action plan and pricing estimate for Dedicated/Burst capacity.

Attachments: SLO-Roadmap.xlsx (outline + proposed warm-pool configs)

Thanks — I’ll leave the traffic sample + schedule to you.

Hey Alex — thanks for the csv, that helps a lot. Quick technical notes and the options we typically recommend for the type of burst profile you shared:

1) Warm pools and prewarmed nodes
- We support configurable warm pools (min_warm_nodes) that keep model instances loaded and KV caches populated. Warm nodes serve with ~cold-start-free latency (i.e., within your first-token p95 target).
- Recommended configuration for your profile: set min_warm_nodes to cover ~2x baseline concurrent streams (so ~120 baseline -> warm pool for ~240 streams). This handles most marketing bursts instantly.

2) Scale-up / provisioning behavior
- If demand exceeds the warm pool, we scale by bringing up additional instances. Typical provisioning to usable state: ~45–90s depending on model size and GPU type.
- While new instances are provisioning we have two mechanisms: short-term queuing (configurable queue depth + per-request timeout) and fallback routing to a lower-capacity model variant (e.g., quantized or a smaller architecture) if configured.

3) Queueing and failure semantics
- Default behavior is to queue short-lived requests up to the configured queue depth (we recommend <= 30s request timeout for interactive UX). If queueing exceeds the threshold we can either return 429/503 or route to the fallback variant.
- We can also set a progressive shedding policy: 1) try warm pool, 2) queue for up to Xs, 3) route to fallback if available, 4) finally return an error.

4) Streaming and batching impact
- Continuous batching improves throughput but can add ~10–20ms median overhead and potentially affects tail latency. For interactive streaming (your case), we bias towards lower batching windows and keep streaming chunk sizes small to preserve first-token latency.
- KV cache (prefix caching) helps especially for repeated prompts and chat-heavy flows — warm nodes keep caches hot so repeated users see much lower p95.

5) SLA / burst capacity options
- For customers who need contractual burst guarantees we provide Dedicated reserved capacity and a Burst overlay (pre-allocated, billable capacity that sits above reserved baseline). Without reserved capacity, we rely on warm pool sizing and best-effort cloud provisioning — we can size warm pools to meet most bursts but can't contractually guarantee unlimited burst without a reserved commit.

Attachments: redwood-performance-kit.pdf (overview + recommended configs)
